majordes: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the intelligence of machines or software, as opposed to the intelligence of humans or animals. It is a field of study in computer science that develops and studies intelligent machines. Such machines may be called AIs.

AI technology is widely used throughout industry, government, and science. Some high-profile applications are: advanced web search engines (e.g., Google Search), recommendation systems (used by YouTube, Amazon, and Netflix), understanding human speech (such as Google Assistant, Siri, and Alexa), self-driving cars (e.g., Waymo), generative and creative tools (ChatGPT and AI art), and superhuman play and analysis in strategy games (such as chess and Go).

majordes: Functional materials are generally characterised as those materials which possess particular native properties and functions of their own. For example, ferroelectricity, piezoelectricity, magnetism or energy storage functions.

Functional materials are found in all classes of materials: ceramics, metals, polymers and organic molecules. Functional materials are often used in electromagnetic applications from KHz to THz and at optical frequencies where the plasmonic properties of metals assume particular importance. Functional materials are also of critical importance in materials for energy such as electro- and magnetocaloric materials, for energy storage and for solar harvesting functions.

WhyMe.description:
I adapt quickly when a project requires me to move beyond what I already know.

1. My strongest foundation was originally in React, TypeScript and frontend engineering, but real projects repeatedly pushed me into backend, cloud and infrastructure work. Instead of limiting myself to my existing stack, I learned .NET Minimal APIs, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Docker, AWS ECS/RDS/S3, Terraform and CI/CD as the work required them. At KONGFU Dumpling, this allowed me to contribute across the full system rather than treating the frontend as an isolated layer, eventually working on APIs, database integration, deployment infrastructure and production operations. The backend achieved sub-200ms median API response times under typical workloads.

2. I learn fastest when there is a concrete engineering problem to solve. On Rewowo, I worked across Next.js, FastAPI, PostgreSQL/RDS, S3 and Firebase. When a voucher redemption workflow became too slow under bulk processing, I did not simply search for a new library or rewrite the feature. I first traced where the time was being spent, identified repeated database operations as the main bottleneck, and changed the implementation toward batch validation and updates. The result was roughly a 10x improvement in response speed.

3. My approach to learning is practical and delivery-oriented. I usually begin by understanding the system boundary, reading documentation, building a small working path, then validating it through logs, tests and real behaviour. I also use AI-assisted development tools to accelerate exploration, debugging and unfamiliar APIs, but I treat generated suggestions as hypotheses that still need to be understood and verified. For me, learning a technology is only complete when I can use it safely in a real product.

I value ownership more than simply completing assigned tickets. When I take responsibility for a feature or system, I try to understand what needs to happen from requirement to production and what could prevent the result from being reliable after release.

1. At KONGFU Dumpling, I worked on a full-stack digital menu and advertising platform using Next.js, .NET Minimal APIs, PostgreSQL/Supabase, Docker, AWS and Terraform. The work was not limited to implementing individual UI components. I had to think about API behaviour, data flow, deployment, infrastructure and what happened when the system was running unattended in a real business environment. One practical example was the advertising playback system. Instead of assuming playback would always remain healthy after deployment, I introduced recovery behaviour around interrupted playback, which reduced advertising interruptions by around 70%.

2. At Bluesky Creations, I worked across products including Rewowo and Leave Admin, where features regularly crossed frontend, backend and infrastructure boundaries. On Rewowo, I contributed to the migration and optimisation of a Next.js application, worked with FastAPI and AWS-backed services, and investigated performance problems rather than treating them as someone else's responsibility. The application reached Lighthouse scores above 90 with Total Blocking Time below 70ms after optimisation work.

3. Ownership also means leaving a system easier to operate than I found it. I pay attention to deployment workflows, reusable components, failure handling and technical debt that repeatedly slows future work. I do not believe leadership requires a management title. In engineering, leadership often means noticing an important problem, making the problem clear, proposing a workable path, and staying responsible until the result is actually delivered.

I see communication in software engineering as the ability to reduce ambiguity between people, systems and requirements. Good communication is not only about speaking clearly; it is about making sure that different people are solving the same problem with the same assumptions.

1. Across my professional work, I have often worked between frontend and backend boundaries. At Wolli Software, I built React and Next.js interfaces while integrating with .NET, Node.js and GraphQL services as well as third-party platforms including Stripe, Shopify, Mapbox and Twilio. This required me to understand API contracts, loading and error states, data shapes and edge cases rather than simply waiting for a finished backend and connecting it mechanically.

2. My full-stack work strengthened this further. When working on Rewowo and later KONGFU Dumpling, I increasingly had to translate a product requirement into both UI behaviour and backend behaviour. That means asking questions such as: What should happen when this request fails? Which layer should validate the data? What does the user see while the operation is processing? What needs to be logged when production behaviour is different from local development? Thinking in this way helps prevent frontend and backend implementations from drifting apart.

3. I also try to make technical communication concrete. When discussing a problem, I prefer to show a reproduction case, measurable behaviour, logs, screenshots, API responses or a small implementation rather than relying on vague opinions. My earlier experience in public speaking, debate and presentations helped me become comfortable explaining ideas, but my professional experience taught me the more important lesson: effective engineering communication is about clarity, context and helping the team make the next decision faster.

My preferred way to solve engineering problems is to reduce them from a vague symptom into something measurable, identify the actual bottleneck, and then make the smallest change that solves the underlying cause.

1. A good example came from the Rewowo voucher redemption workflow. The system needed to validate voucher status, expiry and policy rules before completing redemption. During testing with around 100 vouchers in one operation, the response time exceeded 10 seconds. Rather than immediately rewriting the API, I narrowed the problem down to backend database access and found an N+1-style pattern where validation and updates were being performed repeatedly for individual records. I changed the workflow to use batch queries and updates, including WHERE IN-style operations, reducing unnecessary database round trips. The resulting workflow was around 10x faster.

2. I have applied the same reasoning to frontend and delivery problems. At Wolli Software, optimisation work contributed to roughly a 20% improvement in Core Web Vitals, around a 30% reduction in frontend errors and approximately a 50% reduction in CI/CD execution time. These results came from treating performance and reliability as engineering problems that could be observed and decomposed, rather than as general goals such as 'make the website faster'.

3. I also try to separate symptoms from causes during production debugging. If something fails after deployment, I first ask whether the problem comes from code, environment configuration, network behaviour, data, deployment state or an external service. I reproduce the smallest failing path, inspect the available evidence, change one important variable at a time and verify the result. This approach helps me stay systematic even when the original issue appears complicated.

I care about the quality of what users actually experience. For me, frontend craftsmanship is not simply making an interface visually attractive; it includes hierarchy, responsiveness, interaction, consistency, accessibility, performance and how confidently a user can understand what to do next.

1. React and Next.js remain my strongest area, and much of my professional work has involved building reusable interfaces for real products rather than isolated demonstration pages. I have worked with component-driven architectures, Redux and Zustand state management, Tailwind, Ant Design and reusable UI patterns across desktop, mobile and large-screen experiences. At Bluesky Creations, optimisation work on Rewowo helped achieve Lighthouse scores above 90 and Total Blocking Time below 70ms, because I believe a polished interface should also feel fast.

2. At Wolli Software, I worked on frontend performance and maintainability across production applications. This included reusable component patterns, responsive interfaces, integrations and performance improvements that contributed to better Core Web Vitals. I learned that UI quality often comes from dozens of small engineering decisions: preventing unnecessary renders, handling loading states properly, designing predictable component APIs, keeping spacing and typography consistent, and ensuring edge cases do not destroy the layout.

3. My visual-design background still influences how I work, but I now apply it through a product-engineering lens. I pay close attention to alignment, visual hierarchy, typography and interaction details, while also asking whether the design is maintainable and whether it helps the user complete their task. I want the final result to look intentional, but more importantly, I want it to behave intentionally.

Under Pressure, I try to remain systematic when software behaves differently from what was expected, especially when the problem appears in production and there is pressure to restore service quickly.

1. Through Rewowo, Leave Admin and KONGFU Dumpling, I have dealt with deployment failures, production differences and features that behaved correctly locally but required further investigation after deployment. Working with Vercel, GitHub Actions, Docker and AWS taught me that production debugging is often less about writing new code and more about carefully locating which assumption has broken across application code, environment variables, build configuration, infrastructure, external services or runtime data.

2. One example is the digital advertising system at KONGFU Dumpling. A TV-facing application has a different reliability requirement from a normal website because it may need to run for long periods without someone actively refreshing or supervising it. I worked on recovery behaviour so that playback could recover automatically from interruptions rather than depending on manual intervention. This reduced playback interruptions by around 70% and reinforced an important lesson for me: a production feature is not finished when the happy path works; it is finished when common failure paths have also been considered.

3. When something goes wrong, I try not to jump between random fixes. I reproduce the issue, collect evidence, isolate the failing layer, communicate what is known and unknown, make the smallest safe change, and then verify both the fix and possible regressions. Reliability, to me, means being someone a team can trust to keep thinking clearly when the system is not behaving clearly.

当项目需要我走出已有技术边界时，我能够快速学习并把新技术真正用于交付，而不只是停留在“了解过”。

1. 我的技术优势最初主要集中在 React、TypeScript 和前端开发，但真实项目不断要求我向后端、云服务和基础设施扩展。随着工作的需要，我逐渐学习并实际使用 .NET Minimal API、FastAPI、PostgreSQL、Docker、AWS ECS/RDS/S3、Terraform 和 CI/CD。在 KONGFU Dumpling 的项目中，我已经不再只关注前端页面，而是参与 API、数据库集成、部署基础设施以及生产环境运行，最终使主要 API 在典型生产负载下保持低于 200ms 的中位响应时间。

2. 我学习效率最高的时候，通常不是单纯学习一个框架，而是面前存在一个明确的工程问题。例如在 Rewowo 的 Voucher Redeem 功能中，一次处理约 100 张 Voucher 时响应超过 10 秒。我先定位性能时间到底消耗在哪里，最终发现主要问题来自数据库重复查询和更新。我随后将逐条处理改为批量校验和批量更新，大幅减少数据库往返，最终使整个流程的响应速度提高约 10 倍。

3. 我的学习方式始终以交付为导向。我通常会先理解系统边界和核心概念，再阅读官方文档，快速搭建一条最小可运行路径，并通过日志、测试和实际行为验证理解是否正确。我也会使用 AI 辅助工具提高探索陌生技术、排查问题和阅读 API 的效率，但我不会直接相信生成结果，而是把它作为待验证的假设。对我来说，真正学会一项技术意味着我已经可以在真实项目中安全地使用它。

相比只完成被分配的开发任务，我更看重对最终结果负责。当我接手一个功能或系统时，我会尽量理解它从需求、实现、部署到生产运行的完整链路，以及上线之后什么问题可能真正影响业务。

1. 在 KONGFU Dumpling，我参与并负责一个基于 Next.js、.NET Minimal API、PostgreSQL/Supabase、Docker、AWS 和 Terraform 的数字菜单及广告系统。工作内容并不只是完成某几个页面，而是需要同时考虑 API 行为、数据流、部署、基础设施以及系统在真实门店长期无人值守运行时会发生什么。广告播放就是一个典型例子。我没有假设部署成功之后视频就永远能够正常播放，而是针对播放中断设计自动恢复机制，使广告播放中断减少约 70%。

2. 在 Bluesky Creations，我参与 Rewowo、Leave Admin 等不同产品，很多需求天然横跨前端、后端和部署环境。在 Rewowo 中，我不仅进行 Next.js 页面开发，还参与 FastAPI、AWS 服务集成和性能排查。经过优化，页面 Lighthouse 达到 90+，Total Blocking Time 控制在 70ms 以下。对我来说，看到性能问题之后主动继续追查，比简单地认为“后端慢”或“部署不是我的职责”更重要。

3. 我认为工程上的领导力不一定意味着拥有 Manager 的职位。它更多体现为：发现一个重要问题、把问题描述清楚、提出现实可行的方案，并持续跟进直到结果真正交付。同时，我也会关注部署流程、可复用组件、异常处理和那些会不断拖慢未来开发的技术债，因为真正的 Ownership 不只是让今天的功能上线，也包括让明天维护它的人更轻松。

我理解的软件工程沟通，本质上是减少人与人之间、前后端之间以及需求与实现之间的歧义。好的沟通不只是“会表达”，而是让不同的人对正在解决的问题拥有一致的理解和假设。

1. 我的职业经历中有大量工作处于前后端交界处。在 Wolli Software，我使用 React、Next.js 开发界面的同时，还需要对接 .NET、Node.js、GraphQL 服务，以及 Stripe、Shopify、Mapbox、Twilio 等第三方平台。这要求我理解的不只是页面怎么展示，还包括 API contract、数据结构、loading/error state、边界情况以及第三方服务出现异常时用户最终会看到什么。

2. 随着我逐渐承担更多 Full-Stack 工作，这种能力变得更加重要。在 Rewowo 和 KONGFU Dumpling 等项目中，我经常需要把一个业务需求同时转化为前端行为和后端行为。我会主动思考：请求失败之后页面应该发生什么？哪些数据应该由后端验证？用户等待期间看到什么？生产环境出现异常时需要记录哪些信息？这些问题能够减少前端和后端分别按照不同假设实现之后再返工的情况。

3. 我也尽量让技术沟通建立在事实而不是感觉上。讨论问题时，我更愿意提供复现步骤、日志、截图、API Response、性能数据或一个最小实现，而不是只说“这里好像有问题”。我过去参与演讲、辩论和展示的经历让我不害怕表达观点，而真正进入职场之后，我逐渐理解到更重要的事情是：提供足够的上下文，让团队能够更快地做出下一个正确决策。

我解决工程问题时，更习惯先把一个模糊的“现象”转化为可以观察和测量的问题，找到真正的瓶颈，再使用尽可能小但有效的改动解决根因，而不是直接开始重写代码。

1. Rewowo 的 Voucher Redeem API 是一个很典型的例子。业务需要在兑换前检查 Voucher 的状态、有效期以及相关规则。在一次处理约 100 张 Voucher 的测试中，接口响应超过了 10 秒。我没有立即重构整个系统，而是逐步排查请求时间消耗，最终定位到数据库访问存在类似 N+1 的问题：系统需要重复对单条记录进行查询和更新。我把这一流程调整为批量查询和批量更新，例如使用 WHERE IN 一次性取得需要的数据，大幅减少数据库 IO 和 round trip。最终整个 Redemption 流程响应速度提高约 10 倍。

2. 同样的方法也被我用于前端和工程流程优化。在 Wolli Software，我参与的性能与工程优化最终带来了约 20% 的 Core Web Vitals 改善、约 30% 的前端错误下降，以及约 50% 的 CI/CD 时间缩短。这些改进并不是从“让网站快一点”这种模糊目标出发，而是将问题拆分成渲染、网络请求、错误来源以及构建流程中的具体瓶颈，再逐项处理。

3. 生产问题排查时，我也会尽量区分“症状”和“原因”。一个部署后的问题可能来自业务代码，也可能来自环境变量、构建配置、网络、数据库、部署状态或者第三方服务。我通常会先建立最小复现路径，检查已有证据，再一次改变一个关键变量，并验证修复后的行为。这种方式让我面对复杂问题时仍然能够保持一个相对稳定、可解释的推理过程。

我很在意用户最终真正感受到的产品质量。对我来说，Frontend Craftsmanship 不只是把界面做得漂亮，它同时包括信息层级、响应式体验、交互反馈、一致性、性能以及用户能不能快速理解下一步应该做什么。

1. React 和 Next.js 一直是我最擅长的方向之一，我的大部分职业经历也是在真实产品中构建可维护的 UI，而不是单独制作 Demo。我使用过 Redux、Zustand、Tailwind、Ant Design，并围绕不同项目构建过可复用的组件和状态管理方案，同时处理桌面端、移动端以及大屏/电视等不同使用场景。在 Bluesky Creations 的 Rewowo 项目中，我参与性能优化后使 Lighthouse 达到 90+，并将 Total Blocking Time 控制到 70ms 以下，因为我认为一个真正精致的页面不仅应该看起来好，也应该真正感觉快。

2. 在 Wolli Software，我长期参与生产环境 React/Next.js 应用的开发、维护和性能优化。工作内容让我逐渐认识到 UI 的品质往往来自很多并不起眼的工程决策：减少不必要的渲染、正确处理 loading 和 error state、保持组件 API 一致、确保 spacing 和 typography 稳定，以及保证异常数据不会轻易破坏布局。这些细节共同决定了一个产品到底显得可靠还是粗糙。

3. 我过去的美术、设计和视觉表达经验现在仍然影响着我的开发方式，但它已经从单纯追求“好看”变成了更加工程化的产品思维。我依然会关注对齐、层级、字体、留白和交互细节，但同时也会问：这个设计是否容易维护？是否能复用？是否真的让用户更容易完成任务？我希望最终产品看起来是经过认真设计的，同时它的行为也应该同样经过认真设计。

当软件表现与预期不一致时，尤其问题已经发生在生产环境，我会尽量保持系统化的排查方式，而不是因为上线压力而不断尝试随机修改。

1. 在 Rewowo、Leave Admin 和 KONGFU Dumpling 等项目中，我都遇到过部署失败、生产环境差异以及本地工作正常但部署之后需要进一步排查的问题。Vercel、GitHub Actions、Docker 和 AWS 的实际使用让我逐渐意识到，生产 Debugging 很多时候并不是马上写更多代码，而是首先找出到底是哪一个假设失效了：业务代码、环境变量、Build Configuration、基础设施、外部服务还是 Runtime Data。

2. KONGFU Dumpling 的电视广告系统给了我一个很具体的 Reliability 场景。电视端应用和普通网页不同，它可能需要长时间运行，而且不会始终有人站在旁边刷新页面。一旦播放中断，单纯让功能在 Happy Path 下工作并不够。因此我为播放流程加入自动恢复逻辑，让系统在部分异常情况下能够自己恢复，而不是依赖人工重新操作。最终广告播放中断减少约 70%。这件事情让我更加明确：生产功能真正完成的标准，不是正常路径可以运行，而是常见异常也已经被认真考虑。

3. 当出现问题时，我通常会按照一个比较稳定的顺序处理：复现问题、收集证据、定位失败层级、区分已经确定和仍然未知的信息、进行最小且安全的修改，然后重新验证修复和可能产生的回归。我理解的可靠性，是当系统本身变得不确定时，团队仍然可以相信我会保持清晰、有条理地继续推进问题。
